findings.description: Economic Impact Letter template presents 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act reduced Medicaid coverage by $990 billion (gross), removing the safety net for approximately 10 million Americans (CBO projection)' as an established fact but provides no citation URL. Adjacent claims in the same template cite Yale Budget Lab and EPI with hyperlinks. The uneven evidentiary standard means letter-writers cannot verify the CBO figure before submitting correspondence, and the past-tense 'reduced' presents the legislative outcome as settled without grounding.
findings.suggestion: Add a direct citation URL for the CBO projection (e.g., the specific CBO cost-estimate release for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) alongside the Yale Budget Lab and EPI citations already present. If the bill's status is uncertain, add a hedge: 'the proposed One Big Beautiful Bill Act would reduce...' with the CBO score linked.
findings.context: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act reduced Medicaid coverage by $990 billion (gross), removing the safety net for approximately 10 million Americans (CBO projection).

findings.description: Body text: 'Research by McKinsey Global Institute suggests women face higher automation exposure than men in several developed economies, partly because of occupational concentration in these categories.' No report year, edition, or URL appears in the body. The epistemic flag at the end of the article addresses confidence but not citability — a reader who wants to follow the citation has no anchor. In an article otherwise strong on epistemic discipline, this claim floats without a traceable source.
findings.suggestion: Add the report title and year in the body text — e.g., 'McKinsey Global Institute (2019, The Future of Women at Work)' — and link to the OHCHR or McKinsey publication. The epistemic flag can remain as a caveat about current-edition validity.
findings.context: Research by McKinsey Global Institute suggests women face higher automation exposure than men in several developed economies, partly because of occupational concentration in these categories.

findings.description: Body text uses assertive framing: 'Research on prior automation waves documents elevated mental health effects among displaced workers: increased depression rates, elevated substance use, reduced life expectancy in affected cohorts.' The verb 'documents' presents the claim as settled and multi-sourced. The epistemic flag at the article footer says 'specific studies not cited; verify against peer-reviewed literature before academic use.' The gap between 'documents' (body) and 'not cited' (footer) constitutes a fair-witness inconsistency — the body claims more certainty than the epistemic flag sustains.
findings.suggestion: Soften the body verb from 'documents' to 'suggests' or 'indicates', or add a canonical citation (e.g., Case & Deaton 2015, or Autor et al. on labor market polarization) directly in the body. The epistemic flag can remain but should not be the primary correction for a body-text overclaim.
findings.context: Research on prior automation waves documents elevated mental health effects among displaced workers: increased depression rates, elevated substance use, reduced life expectancy in affected cohorts.

findings.description: Researcher Letter template: 'productivity-pay gap has widened by a factor of 3.5 since 1979 (Economic Policy Institute)' — cites EPI with a hyperlink, which constitutes good practice. However the hyperlink points to a general EPI page rather than the specific report containing the 3.5x figure. If the EPI methodology or figure changes, letter-writers using this template in future would misrepresent the source. Low severity because citation exists; medium risk as this figure appears in correspondence submitted to elected officials.
findings.suggestion: Replace the general EPI homepage link with the specific chart or report URL (EPI Productivity-Pay Gap chart, currently at https://www.epi.org/productivity-pay-gap/) or cite the specific report (Bivens & Mishel, 2015, Understanding the Historic Divergence). This anchors the 3.5x claim to a verifiable source.
findings.context: The productivity-pay gap has widened by a factor of 3.5 since 1979 (Economic Policy Institute).
